sentence: Some anxiety is a normal part of life; it becomes a concern when worry is hard to control and gets in the way of daily life.
note: NHS: some anxiety is normal, see a GP if it affects daily life or causes distress.

sentence: Adults are usually advised to try psychological treatment, such as cognitive behavioural therapy, before medicine.
note: NHS summary: psychological treatment before medication; CBT one of the most effective.

sentence: People in England can refer themselves to an NHS talking therapies service without seeing a GP first.
note: NHS: you can refer yourself to an NHS talking therapies service without a GP referral.

sentence: If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 offer urgent support.
note: Crisis route, see final section.

sentence: Feeling anxious now and then is part of life, and the NHS says some anxiety is normal.
note: NHS: 'Some anxiety is normal'.

sentence: Generalised anxiety disorder, or GAD, is a long-term condition in which a person feels worried or stressed much of the time, about many things, in a way that is hard to control.
note: Core problem described as worry/stress hard to control that interferes with daily life; 'long-term' and 'many things' not separately quoted - flagged for second pass.

sentence: That worry gets in the way of daily life.
note: NHS summary of core problem.

sentence: Alongside worry, the NHS lists sleep difficulties, restlessness or irritability, tiredness, muscle tension, stomach problems, palpitations (a pounding or fluttering heartbeat), dizziness and low mood.
note: NHS symptom list: sleep difficulties, restlessness/irritability, tiredness, tension, stomach problems, palpitations, dizziness, low mood.

sentence: Because many of these also occur in other conditions, a GP can help work out what is going on.
note: Inference from 'see a GP' advice; flagged for second pass.

sentence: The exact cause of GAD is not fully understood, and several factors probably combine.
note: Sources: exact cause not fully understood; several factors likely combine.

sentence: Factors named in the sources include inherited genes, past stressful or traumatic experiences, a long-term painful health condition, and past drug or alcohol misuse.
note: Listed causes in NHS/NHS inform pages.

sentence: NICE advises a full assessment that looks at how many symptoms there are, how severe they are, how long the current episode has lasted and how the condition has developed over time.
note: NICE CG113 assessment appendix.

sentence: The GP also asks about distress, the effect on daily functioning, and any past history of anxiety and mood disorders.
note: NICE.

sentence: Where another condition such as depression is also present, NICE says the more severe disorder is generally treated first.
note: NICE.

sentence: A short two-question screen about feelings of anxiety and the ability to control worry may be used.
note: NICE: GAD-2.

sentence: Adults are usually advised to try psychological treatment before medication.
note: NHS: psychological treatment before medicine.

sentence: Cognitive behavioural therapy, or CBT, is a talking therapy that looks at how thoughts, feelings and actions affect one another.
note: Definition of CBT (textbook).

sentence: The NHS describes CBT as one of the most effective treatments for GAD, and CBT and applied relaxation are both available on the NHS.
note: Retrieved: CBT one of the most effective; CBT and applied relaxation on NHS.

sentence: NICE describes CBT-based self-help as a first, low-intensity step, with the materials worked through step by step over several weeks.
note: NICE CG113: CBT-based self-help, systematic, at least 6 weeks.

sentence: If talking therapy is not enough, medicine is the next option, and the usual first choice is an SSRI, a type of antidepressant.
note: NHS: SSRI antidepressant usual first choice if talking therapy not enough.

sentence: NICE sets out treatment in steps, starting with identification, assessment, education about the condition and treatment options, and active monitoring.
note: NICE step 1.

sentence: Step 4 is for complex, treatment-resistant anxiety with marked impairment or a high risk of self-harm, and involves specialist care.
note: NICE step 4.

sentence: NHS self-help ideas include regular exercise, relaxation or breathing practice, cutting back on caffeine, which can disrupt sleep, and eating well.
note: NHS self-help page list.

sentence: The NHS advises against turning to alcohol, cigarettes, gambling or drugs to relieve anxiety.
note: NHS: avoid alcohol, cigarettes, gambling, drugs as a way to relieve anxiety.

sentence: Many books and courses can teach ways of coping with anxiety.
note: NHS self-help page.

sentence: The NHS says to see a GP if anxiety is affecting daily life or causing distress.
note: NHS: see a GP if anxiety affects daily life or causes distress.

sentence: A GP can talk through treatment and refer on, and people can also refer themselves directly to an NHS talking therapies service.
note: NHS self-referral.

sentence: Charities such as Mind, Rethink Mental Illness and Anxiety UK also offer support.
note: NHS page lists these charities.

sentence: Anxiety is common and treatable, and most people will not need emergency help. If things feel unmanageable, these routes are open.
note: Assignment brief: every mental-health page carries the crisis route; trust pages (gmmh urgent-help) list NHS urgent mental health support alongside 999.

sentence: If you or someone else is in immediate danger, or has been physically harmed, call 999 or go to A&E.
note: Trust pages: if life is at risk, someone is in immediate danger or has harmed themselves, call 999 or go to A&E.

sentence: For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), which trusts describe as available at any time, for yourself or on someone else's behalf.
note: NHS trust page: call NHS 111 option 2 for urgent mental health support; 24/7; can call for yourself or someone else.

sentence: Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.
note: Samaritans 116 123 free, 24 hours: returned in the urgent-help and NHS grief searches.
